title: Least-Recently-Used Cache
statement:
Build a key–value cache with a fixed capacity. When it is full and a new key arrives, it throws out the key that was used least recently. Both reading and writing a key count as using it.

  • LRUCache(capacity) creates an empty cache that holds at most capacity keys.
  • get(key) returns the value stored for key, or -1 if the key is not in the cache.
  • put(key, value) stores the value, replacing an older value for the same key. If this adds a key to a full cache, first remove the least recently used key.

Both operations must run in O(1) average time.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the cache. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: get(1) makes key 1 the most recent, so when key 3 arrives in a full cache, key 2 is the one evicted.
Writing an existing key replaces its value and does not evict anything.

constraints: At most 200 000 calls to get and put
hints: A hash map gives O(1) lookup by key, but it does not remember order of use. What structure lets you move one item to the front and drop the last one in O(1)?
A doubly linked list ordered from most to least recently used can unlink any node in O(1) — if you can find the node. Store the nodes themselves in the map.
Sentinel head and tail nodes remove every empty-list special case.

explain.intuition:
You need two things at once: find a key instantly, and know which key is the oldest. A hash map does the first, a list ordered by recency does the second. Combine them: the map points into a doubly linked list, so any node can be unlinked and moved to the front in O(1), and the node at the back is always the one to evict.

In JavaScript and Python there is a shortcut: Map and dict remember insertion order, so deleting and re-inserting a key moves it to the end. Interviewers usually want the linked-list version, because it shows you understand what that shortcut does.
steps: Keep a doubly linked list with two sentinel nodes, head (most recent side) and tail (least recent side), plus a map from key to node.
get(key): if the key is missing return -1. Otherwise unlink its node, insert it right after head, and return its value.
put(key, value): if the key exists, update the value and move the node to the front.
Otherwise, if the cache is full, take the node just before tail, unlink it and delete its key from the map. Then create the new node, put it in the map and insert it after head.
pitfalls: Forgetting that get also counts as a use and must move the node to the front.
Updating an existing key's value without moving it to the front.
Evicting before checking whether the key already exists — overwriting a key in a full cache must not evict anything.

solutions.title: Ordered map shortcut
solutions.idea: Map (JS) and dict (Python) iterate in insertion order. Re-inserting a key moves it to the end, and the first key is the least recently used one.

solutions.title: Hash map + doubly linked list
solutions.idea: The version interviewers expect. The map finds a node in O(1); the list keeps nodes in order of use, with sentinels at both ends.

followups: Make it safe to call from many threads at once. Where do you need a lock, and can reads avoid it?
Evict the least frequently used key instead (LFU). Which extra structure keeps that O(1)?
